1.q: וִ⁠יהוֹרָ֣ם בֶּן־אַחְאָ֗ב מָלַ֤ךְ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ בְּ⁠שֹׁ֣מְר֔וֹן בִּ⁠שְׁנַת֙ שְׁמֹנֶ֣ה עֶשְׂרֵ֔ה לִ⁠יהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה וַ⁠יִּמְלֹ֖ךְ שְׁתֵּים־עֶשְׂרֵ֥ה שָׁנָֽה
1.note: In this verse and the next two verses, the author is introducing **Jehoram** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Israel**. In the preceding book of 1 Kings, the author introduced each new king in this same way, and he will introduce each new king this way throughout this book. It would be good to show this in your translation by representing his characteristic phrases the same way each time. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated these phrases in 1 Kings 15:1 and similar instances throughout that book.

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **18**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat’s reign]

2.note: See how you translated the similar expression “in your eyes” in 1:13. Alternate translation: [And he did what Yahweh considered to be evil]

The author is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean things of a certain kind. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [evil things] or [what was evil]

3.note: The author is speaking of Jehoram continuing to do sinful things as if he had **clung** to them physically. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he persisted in the sins of Jeroboam] or [he continued to commit the sins of Jeroboam]
Since the pronoun **it** refers back to the **sins** of Jeroboam, it may be more natural in your language to use a plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [He did not turn away from them]

The author is speaking of Jehoram’s continuing sins as if they were something he could have turned away from physically. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He did not stop committing them] or [He did not abandon them]

4.q: וּ⁠מֵישַׁ֥ע מֶֽלֶךְ־מוֹאָ֖ב הָיָ֣ה נֹקֵ֑ד וְ⁠הֵשִׁ֤יב לְ⁠מֶֽלֶךְ־יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מֵאָה־אֶ֣לֶף כָּרִ֔ים וּ⁠מֵ֥אָה אֶ֖לֶף אֵילִ֥ים צָֽמֶר
4.note: Here the author is providing background information about **Mesha** and his relationship with Israel to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

5.note: See how you translated the similar expression in [2:1](ta:02).

6.note: The author is using the term **day** to mean a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at that time]

See the discussion in the Introduction to 2 Kings of how the author and characters often use the name of a nation, tribe, or city to represent its army. Alternate translation: [the whole Israelite army]

7.note: In this context, the author does not mean that Jehoram **went** somewhere. He means that he took the action that he describes next. Alternate translation: [And he took action]

See the discussion of this term in the Introduction to 2 Kings. In contexts such as this, it introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this phrase explicitly, here or in its other instances in the book.
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:3. Alternate translation: [I will go]

7.q: כָּמ֧וֹ⁠נִי כָמ֛וֹ⁠ךָ כְּ⁠עַמִּ֥⁠י כְ⁠עַמֶּ֖⁠ךָ כְּ⁠סוּסַ֥⁠י כְּ⁠סוּסֶֽי⁠ךָ
7.note: Jehoshaphat is using a common expression of his culture to agree to join Jehoram in an attack against Moab. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Kings 22:4, where Jehoshaphat says the same thing to Jehoram’s father Ahab. Alternate translation: [I and my army with its horses will fight alongside you and your army with its horses]

8.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Jehoram in the first instance in this verse, while it refers to Jehoshaphat in the second instance. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Jehoram said … And Jehoshaphat replied]

Jehoram is using **Where is this, the way we shall go up** as a common expression of his culture to ask what **way** or route they should take. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [By what way should we go up]

9.note: The author assumes that readers will understand that by **they went around**, he means that these armies went around the southern end of the Dead Sea. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. You may wish to use the name that this body of water had in biblical times, “the Sea of the Arabah.” Alternate translation: [and they went around the Dead Sea] or [and they went around the Sea of the Arabah]

Here, **the camp** represents the soldiers who were camped there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the soldiers]

The author is using the expression **at their feet** to represent that these **animals** were walking behind the soldiers as they marched. As 3:16 suggests, these probably included cattle to eat, horses to ride into battle, and animals to carry supplies. Alternate translation: [that were walking behind them]

10.note: The king of Israel is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, dismay or distress. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what the king of Israel was feeling, or you could say what made him distressed. Alternate translation: [What a disaster] or [This makes me distressed]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [It certainly appears that]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 13. Alternate translation: [into the power of Moab]

11.note: See how you decided at 1:10 to represent the phrase **and said** when it introduces a direct quotation.

The servant is using **poured water onto the hands of** as a common expression of his culture to mean “served as a personal attendant to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who was a personal attendant of Elijah]

12.note: Here, **the word of Yahweh** represents Yahweh speaking through Elisha. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh speaks through him]

12.q: וַ⁠יֵּרְד֣וּ אֵלָ֗י⁠ו מֶ֧לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל וִ⁠יהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט וּ⁠מֶ֥לֶךְ אֱדֽוֹם
12.note: The tents of these kings were probably on a height overlooking the camp of their soldiers, while Elisha was probably staying down within the camp. The author is marking travel for change in elevation. See how you translated the comparable expression “go up” in 1:3. Alternate translation: [And the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went to him]

13.note: Elisha is using **What to me and to you** as a common expression of his culture to insist that he has nothing in common with the **king of Israel** when it comes to seeking divine guidance. As Elisha notes, King Jehoram worships Baal, and so Elisha says he should ask prophets of Baal to help him rather than a prophet of Yahweh. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 2 Samuel, see how you translated the same expression in 2 Samuel 16:10. Alternate translation: [I want to have nothing to do with your request that I seek divine guidance for you!]

Elisha actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying. He does not actually want the king of Israel to consult false prophets. Rather, he is rebuking him for his idolatry. If, for such a purpose, a speaker of your language would not say the opposite of what he meant, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You had no right to come to me, since you and your family worship false gods]

14.q: חַי־יְהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָמַ֣דְתִּי לְ⁠פָנָ֔י⁠ו כִּ֗י לוּלֵ֛י פְּנֵ֛י יְהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֖ה אֲנִ֣י נֹשֵׂ֑א אִם־אַבִּ֥יט אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אִם־אֶרְאֶֽ⁠ךָּ
14.note: Following the custom of his culture, Elisha is swearing an oath by guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred and by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. In a context such as this, it may be natural to express just the first part of the condition as a negative statement. Alternate translation: [I swear by Yahweh of hosts, to whose face I stand, that unless I were lifting the face of Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah, I would not look at you and I would not regard you]

Here, **to whose face I stand** represents being in the presence of Yahweh and serving him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in whose presence I stand] or [whose servant I am]

14.q: לוּלֵ֛י פְּנֵ֛י יְהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֖ה אֲנִ֣י נֹשֵׂ֑א אִם־אַבִּ֥יט אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ וְ⁠אִם־אֶרְאֶֽ⁠ךָּ
14.note: If it would appear in your language that Elisha was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [I am only looking at you and regarding you because I am lifting the face of Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah]

Elisha is using **lifting the face of** as a common expression of his culture to mean “showing respect to” or “showing favor toward.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [if I did not respect Jehoshaphat]

Elisha is saying he would actually not even **look at** or **regard** the king of Israel. He means that he would not do the slightest thing to help him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I would not do the slightest thing to help you]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I would not even look at you at all]

15.note: The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [when the harpist played]

Here, **hand** represents the power of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that the power of Yahweh came upon him]

16.q: כֹּ֖ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה עָשֹׂ֛ה הַ⁠נַּ֥חַל הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה גֵּבִ֥ים ׀ גֵּבִֽים
16.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says to make this valley ditches, ditches]

The author is repeating the word **ditches** in order to intensify the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Dig ditch after ditch in this valley] or [Make this valley full of ditches]

17.q: כִּֽי־כֹ֣ה ׀ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה לֹֽא־תִרְא֥וּ ר֨וּחַ֙ וְ⁠לֹֽא־תִרְא֣וּ גֶ֔שֶׁם וְ⁠הַ⁠נַּ֥חַל הַ⁠ה֖וּא יִמָּ֣לֵא מָ֑יִם וּ⁠שְׁתִיתֶ֛ם אַתֶּ֥ם וּ⁠מִקְנֵי⁠כֶ֖ם וּֽ⁠בְהֶמְתְּ⁠כֶֽם
17.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh says that you will not see wind, and you will not see rain, but this valley will be filled with water, and you and your cattle and your animals will drink]

Elisha is referring to all of a rainstorm by naming its two major components, **wind** and **rain**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You will not see a rainstorm]

The expression **will be filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but water will fill this valley]

18.note: Elisha is using **in the eyes of Yahweh** as a common expression of his culture to mean “in the judgment of Yahweh” or “from Yahweh’s perspective.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And this is easy from Yahweh’s perspective]
Here, **hand** represents power or control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into your power]

19.note: See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author and characters may use the term “strike” to mean “destroy.” Alternate translation: [And you will destroy]

20.note: The author is using this phrase to introduce a new development within an event. See how you translated the same phrase in 2:9.

The author is speaking of **the grain offering** as if it were a living thing that **went up** by itself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when they offered up the grain offering]
See how you translated the term “behold” in 1:9.

The expression **was filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [and waters filled the land]

21.note: The author is saying **all of Moab** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [And people throughout Moab]

The expression **were summoned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Moabite leaders summoned their soldiers]

Here, **tying a belt** represents being old enough to fight in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from those who were just old enough to bear arms]

22.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they looked red, as if they had been blood]

23.note: The Moabites are repeating forms of the verb “destroy” in order to intensify their expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [The kings have certainly destroyed themselves]

Here, **the kings** represents the opposing kings and the armies they are leading. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The kings have certainly led their armies to fight each other’s armies]
The pronoun **they** refers to the soldiers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and their soldiers have all struck each other]
See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author may use the term “struck” to mean “killed.” Alternate translation: [and they have killed, a man his fellow]

The Moabites are using **a man his fellow** as a common expression of their culture to mean that each soldier has killed his opponent. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they have each killed their opponents] or [and they have all killed each other]

**And now** was an expression that speakers in this culture commonly used to introduce the implications of what they had been saying. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation.
See how you translated the similar expression in [1:1](ta:01). Alternate translation: [you Moabites]

24.note: See how you translated the term “arose” in 3:7. Alternate translation: [and Israel took action]

See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author may use the term “struck” to mean “defeated” or “attacked.” Alternate translation: [and they defeated the Moabite soldiers … and they attacked the kingdom of Moab]
See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author may use the term **face** to put focus on the interaction between people or groups. Alternate translation: [as they opposed them]

It may be more natural in your language to use the noun **Moab** in the first part of this sentence and the pronoun **it** in the second part of the sentence. Alternate translation: [And they came into Moab, and they struck it]

25.note: The author is using **a man his stone** as a common expression of his culture to mean “each of the soldiers threw stones.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and each of the soldiers threw stones on every good portion]

The author is using the pronoun **one** in a general sense, not to refer to a specific person. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [until the only city whose stone walls were still intact was Kir Hareseth]
In this context, the word **struck** has the same meaning as in its second instance in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [and they attacked it]

26.note: The author is speaking of this **battle** as if it had been a living thing that could have been **stronger than** the king of Moab. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he was losing the battle]

27.note: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of what this statement could mean.

The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelite, Judean, and Edomite soldiers. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the Israelite, Judean, and Edomite soldiers departed]
